# Context

A trial has hundreds of photographs. The steps are always the same: analyse **a folder**, build **one row per plot**, join it to the **field book**, validate against a manual measurement, and analyse the trait like any other.

```{r packages}
library(pliman)
library(dplyr)
library(lme4)
```

# A folder of images

The three images only show the structure: they are **not** three plots of a trial. We copy them to a folder and give them plot numbers as file names.

```{r folder}
dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "plots")
dir.create(dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
src <- system.file("tmp_images", package = "pliman")
invisible(file.copy(file.path(src, c("soybean_touch.jpg", "soy_green.jpg", "flax_grains.jpg")),
                    file.path(dir, c("plot_101.jpg", "plot_102.jpg", "plot_103.jpg"))))
list.files(dir)
```

```{r batch}
# HINT: pattern is the text that all the file names have in common
batch <- analyze_objects(pattern = "___", dir_original = dir, plot = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)    # TODO
batch$statistics
# One row per image: n is the number of objects, area_mean the mean area (in pixels)
```

# Join with the field book

```{r field-book}
field_book <- read.csv("data/field_book_demo.csv")
field_book
```

```{r join}
image_traits <- batch$statistics |>
  mutate(plot = as.integer(sub("plot_", "", img))) |>
  select(plot, seed_number = n, seed_area = area_mean)

trial <- field_book |> left_join(image_traits, by = "plot")
trial
```

# Is the image trait good enough?

An image trait must be **valid** (it agrees with a manual measurement), **precise** (its heritability is high enough to select on) and **reproducible** (two photographs of the same sample give the same value).

**Validation by hand.** Count the seeds in `soy_green.jpg` and in `soybean_touch.jpg` yourself, then compare:

```{r validate}
manual <- c(plot_102 = ___, plot_101 = ___)      # TODO: your manual counts (soy_green is plot_102, soybean_touch is plot_101)
automatic <- c(plot_102 = trial$seed_number[trial$plot == 102],
               plot_101 = trial$seed_number[trial$plot == 101])
rbind(manual, automatic)
# You should get 9 and 30 in both rows. In a real trial, use 20 to 50 plots and plot them
# with plot(manual, automatic); abline(0, 1). A distance from the line that is the same for all
# samples is a BIAS (can be corrected); scatter around it is ERROR (cannot).
```

# The image trait enters the mixed model

From here an image trait is **a trait like any other**. We do not have a trial with photographs, so we **pretend** that the 100-seed weight `SW100` of the bean trial of Day 3 came from images. The code is the same for a real image trait: only the column changes.

```{r pretend}
beans <- read.csv("data/Example_Beans.csv") |>
  mutate(rep = factor(rep), line = factor(line), rb = factor(paste(rep, block, sep = ":")))
beans$image_trait <- beans$SW100       # TODO later: replace with your image trait, joined by plot

m <- lmer(image_trait ~ rep + (1 | line) + (1 | rb), data = beans)
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m))
sg <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "line"]; se <- sigma(m)^2
# Heritability on a line-mean basis for 2 replicates (approximate)
round(sg / (sg + se / 2), 2)           # about 0.87
```

**Your findings:** with a heritability this high, would you use the image trait for selection? What would you need to check first? _...write here..._

# Optional: your own photographs

Copy 3 to 5 phone photos to the folder `my_images/` (plain background, even light, a reference object, file names `plot_201.jpg` and so on). Run `analyze_objects(pattern = "plot_", dir_original = "my_images", plot = TRUE, marker = "id", reference = TRUE, reference_area = ...)` and **look at every labelled image** before you trust the numbers.
